entry.title: The Continuity Equation
entry.content:
This post was revised with the help of ChatGPT.

This post walks through the continuity equation [1], from physical intuition to the mathematical statement. We derive it step by step and explain every quantity involved.

1. Motivation: conservation in physical systems

Many physical quantities are conserved, for example:

  • mass in a closed system;
  • charge in electromagnetism;
  • energy in an isolated system;
  • the number of particles in a fluid.

Although these quantities are conserved globally, they vary locally in space and time. To describe their local behavior, we use density functions. A density tells us how much of the conserved quantity there is per unit volume at each point and time:

  • mass density \( ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)\);
  • charge density \( ho_q( oldsymbol{x}, t)\);
  • energy density \(\epsilon( oldsymbol{x}, t)\);
  • particle number density \(n( oldsymbol{x}, t)\).

Each of these is a function \(\mathbb{R}^n imes \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} o \mathbb{R}\).

To model how a density evolves, imagine the quantity being carried by a flow. A tiny fluid parcel at position \( oldsymbol{x}\) and time \(t\) moves with velocity \( oldsymbol{v}( oldsymbol{x}, t)\) and carries the local amount of the quantity with it.

Our goal is a local law describing how the density changes over space and time. This law is the continuity equation.

2. Basic definitions

Let:

  • \( ho( oldsymbol{x}, t): \mathbb{R}^n imes \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} o \mathbb{R}\) be the scalar density of a conserved quantity;
  • \( oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t): \mathbb{R}^n imes \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} o \mathbb{R}^n\) be the flux. Its component along a unit vector \( oldsymbol{n}\) is the amount of the quantity crossing a unit area perpendicular to \( oldsymbol{n}\) per unit time.

When the quantity is transported by a velocity field \( oldsymbol{v}( oldsymbol{x}, t)\), the flux is

\[ oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t) = ho( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, oldsymbol{v}( oldsymbol{x}, t) .\]

In words, flux is density times velocity: how much passes through depends on how much is there and how fast it moves.

Now fix a region \(V \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) with a smooth boundary \(\partial V\).

  • The total amount inside \(V\) at time \(t\) is

    \[Q_V(t) = \int_V ho( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} .\]

  • Its rate of change is

    \[ rac{d}{dt} Q_V(t) = rac{d}{dt} \int_V ho( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} .\]

    Since the quantity is conserved (there are no sources or sinks), this change can only come from flux across the boundary \(\partial V\).

3. Flux across the boundary

Each point \( oldsymbol{x} \in \partial V\) has an outward unit normal \( oldsymbol{n}( oldsymbol{x})\). Let \(dS\) be the surface area element, and let \(d oldsymbol{S} = oldsymbol{n} \, dS\) be the oriented surface element, pointing outward.

The net outflow through \(\partial V\) per unit time is

\[\oint_{\partial V} oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t) \cdot d oldsymbol{S} .\]

The dot product keeps only the component of the flux normal to the surface; flow tangent to the surface does not cross it. The integral is positive when more of the quantity leaves than enters.

Conservation says that the amount inside decreases exactly at the rate it flows out:

\[ rac{d}{dt} \int_V ho( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} = - \oint_{\partial V} oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t) \cdot d oldsymbol{S} .\]

This is the integral form of the conservation law.

4. Gauss’s divergence theorem

To turn the boundary integral into a volume integral, we use the divergence theorem [2]. It holds for a continuously differentiable field \( oldsymbol{J}\):

\[\oint_{\partial V} oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t) \cdot d oldsymbol{S} = \int_V abla \cdot oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} .\]

The theorem says that the total outward flux through the boundary equals the total divergence inside:

  • the left-hand side adds up what flows out of each patch of the surface;
  • the right-hand side adds up the local “spreading out” of the flow at each point inside \(V\).

Substituting into the conservation law gives

\[ rac{d}{dt} \int_V ho( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} = - \int_V abla \cdot oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} .\]

5. From integral form to differential form

If \( ho\) is smooth enough (see Section 8), we may move the time derivative inside the integral:

\[ rac{d}{dt} \int_V ho( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} = \int_V rac{\partial ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)}{\partial t} \, d oldsymbol{x} .\]

Thus

\[\int_V rac{\partial ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)}{\partial t} \, d oldsymbol{x} = - \int_V abla \cdot oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} ,\]

and moving everything to one side,

\[\int_V \left( rac{\partial ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)}{\partial t} + abla \cdot oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t) ight) d oldsymbol{x} = 0 .\]

This holds for every region \(V\). If the integrand \(g = \partial_t ho + abla \cdot oldsymbol{J}\) is continuous, it must vanish pointwise. To see why, suppose \(g( oldsymbol{x}_0, t) > 0\) at some point. By continuity, \(g > 0\) on a small ball \(B\) around \( oldsymbol{x}_0\), and then \(\int_B g \, d oldsymbol{x} > 0\), a contradiction. The same argument works if \(g( oldsymbol{x}_0, t) < 0\). Therefore

\[ rac{\partial ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)}{\partial t} + abla \cdot oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t) = 0 .\]

6. The continuity equation

Using \( oldsymbol{J} = ho \, oldsymbol{v}\), we obtain the continuity equation:

\[ egin{equation} rac{\partial ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)}{\partial t} + abla \cdot ig( ho( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, oldsymbol{v}( oldsymbol{x}, t) ig) = 0 . \label{eq:continuity} \end{equation}\]

It expresses the local conservation of the quantity carried by the flow.

Expanded form. By the product rule, \( abla \cdot ( ho oldsymbol{v}) = oldsymbol{v} \cdot abla ho + ho \, abla \cdot oldsymbol{v}\), so

\[\underbrace{ rac{\partial ho}{\partial t} + oldsymbol{v} \cdot abla ho}_{\displaystyle rac{D ho}{Dt}} = - ho \, abla \cdot oldsymbol{v} .\]

The left-hand side is the material derivative \(D ho / Dt\), the rate of change of density seen by an observer moving with a parcel. So the density following a parcel changes only when the flow compresses (\( abla \cdot oldsymbol{v} < 0\)) or expands (\( abla \cdot oldsymbol{v} > 0\)). For an incompressible flow (\( abla \cdot oldsymbol{v} = 0\)), the density along each parcel stays constant.

7. Divergence: geometric meaning

The divergence of a vector field is

\[ abla \cdot oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t) = \sum_{i=1}^n rac{\partial J_i( oldsymbol{x}, t)}{\partial x_i} .\]

By the continuity equation, \(\partial_t ho = - abla \cdot oldsymbol{J}\). So:

  • if \( abla \cdot oldsymbol{J} > 0\) at a point, more flows out than in, and \( ho\) decreases there;
  • if \( abla \cdot oldsymbol{J} < 0\), more flows in than out, and \( ho\) increases;
  • if \( abla \cdot oldsymbol{J} = 0\), inflow and outflow balance, and \( ho\) does not change there.

Geometrically, divergence is a local measure of how much a vector field “spreads out” at a point. This follows from the divergence theorem: shrink \(V\) to a small ball \(B_r( oldsymbol{x})\) around a point, and

\[ abla \cdot oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}) = \lim_{r o 0} rac{1}{\lvert B_r vert} \oint_{\partial B_r} oldsymbol{J} \cdot d oldsymbol{S} ,\]

i.e. divergence is the outward flux per unit volume.

8. Why can we swap the derivative and the integral?

We used

\[ rac{d}{dt} \int_V ho( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} = \int_V rac{\partial ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)}{\partial t} \, d oldsymbol{x} .\]

By definition of the derivative,

\[ egin{align*} rac{d}{dt} \int_V ho( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} &= \lim_{\Delta t o 0} rac{1}{\Delta t} \left( \int_V ho( oldsymbol{x}, t + \Delta t) \, d oldsymbol{x} - \int_V ho( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} ight) \[1ex] &= \lim_{\Delta t o 0} \int_V rac{ ho( oldsymbol{x}, t + \Delta t) - ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)}{\Delta t} \, d oldsymbol{x} \[1ex] &\overset{(\star)}{=} \int_V \lim_{\Delta t o 0} rac{ ho( oldsymbol{x}, t + \Delta t) - ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)}{\Delta t} \, d oldsymbol{x} = \int_V rac{\partial ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)}{\partial t} \, d oldsymbol{x} . \end{align*}\]

The step \((\star)\), which swaps the limit and the integral, is the only one that needs justification. A sufficient condition is that \(V\) is bounded and \(\partial_t ho\) is continuous on \(\overline{V} imes [t - \delta, t + \delta]\). By the mean value theorem, the difference quotient equals \(\partial_t ho( oldsymbol{x}, t + heta \Delta t)\) for some \( heta \in (0, 1)\). This is uniformly bounded, so the dominated convergence theorem applies. (The region \(V\) is fixed in time. For a region that moves with the flow, you would need the Reynolds transport theorem instead.)

9. Summary

We began with:

  • a physical idea: a conserved quantity;
  • a model: the quantity is carried by a flow with velocity \( oldsymbol{v}\);
  • a density \( ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)\) and a flux \( oldsymbol{J} = ho oldsymbol{v}\);
  • a balance law: rate of change inside a region = \(-\)(net outflow through its boundary);
  • the divergence theorem: surface integral \( o\) volume integral;
  • swapping derivative and integral: \( rac{d}{dt}\int_V = \int_V \partial_t\);
  • “zero integral over every region” \(\Rightarrow\) “zero integrand.”

We arrived at

\[ rac{\partial ho}{\partial t} + abla \cdot ( ho \, oldsymbol{v}) = 0 .\]

The continuity equation appears whenever we model a conserved quantity moving through space. It captures one simple idea:

Any local change in the quantity must be explained by its flow into or out of that region.

It is fundamental across physics and mathematics: in fluid mechanics, electromagnetism (conservation of charge), quantum mechanics (conservation of probability), and, more recently, in the flow-matching and diffusion models of machine learning, where it describes how a probability density is transported by a learned velocity field.

References

[1] Wikipedia. “Continuity equation.”

[2] Wikipedia. “Divergence theorem.”
entry.summary: Deriving the continuity equation step by step, from conservation laws to the divergence theorem.

entry.title: LC-3 Brief Review
entry.content:
This is a brief review of some topics from ECE 220. All code below is LC-3 assembly; the code blocks use NASM syntax highlighting, which is close enough.

I. Purpose and description

1. Purpose

This program reviews:

  1. LC-3 basics, including I/O;
  2. the run-time stack;
  3. recursion in LC-3;
  4. linked lists in LC-3;
  5. binary trees in LC-3.

2. Description

  1. The program is a direct LC-3 translation of a C program that prints a directory structure.
  2. The directory tree is stored in memory in fixed data structures. The program prints it to the console in a pre-order traversal, in the format shown in Desired output.
  3. To show how C is translated into assembly, every user-defined C function uses the run-time stack. I also wrote my own versions of the OUT and PUTS system calls, which C’s printf() would ultimately rely on. They are called PRINT_A_CHAR and PRINT_A_STRING. Like real system calls, they do not use the run-time stack. They work the same way as the OUT and PUTS trap service routines in the LC-3 operating system.
  4. The test case is not exhaustive. Gemini generated most of it, and I fixed a few syntax errors so that it assembles. Feel free to add more test cases.

3. Data structure design

(1) Files and folders

A file node (a node of a singly linked list):

  • [0] next pointer: the next file in the same folder (NULL if none);
  • [1] pointer to the file name (.STRINGZ).

A folder node (a node of a binary tree):

  • [0] left pointer: the left child (NULL if none);
  • [1] right pointer: the right child (NULL if none);
  • [2] file pointer: the head of this folder’s file list (NULL if none);
  • [3] pointer to the folder name (.STRINGZ).

Both children of a folder are sub-folders of it. The tree is a plain binary tree, not a “left-child, right-sibling” encoding.

(2) Folder tree (test case)

                         root
                /                   \
          projects                  media
          /      \               /         \
    c_project    blog      documents       photos
     /     \                /      \           \
 utils  python_project  reports  presentations  travel
                                                    \
                                                 sub_travel

(3) Files in each folder (test case)

  • root: config.sys
  • projects: README.md
  • c_project: main.c → Makefile
  • utils: helper.c
  • python_project: main.py → requirements.txt
  • blog: index.md
  • media: (empty)
  • documents: meeting_notes.docx → todo_list.txt
  • reports: q1_report.pdf → budget_summary.xlsx
  • presentations: project_kickoff.pptx
  • photos: IMG001.jpg → IMG002.jpg
  • travel: trip.txt → map.png
  • sub_travel: packing_list.md

(4) C structs and function prototypes

4. Desired output

root
    file: config.sys
    projects
        file: README.md
        c_project
            file: main.c Makefile
            utils
                file: helper.c
            python_project
                file: main.py requirements.txt
        blog
            file: index.md
    media
        documents
            file: meeting_notes.docx todo_list.txt
            reports
                file: q1_report.pdf budget_summary.xlsx
            presentations
                file: project_kickoff.pptx
        photos
            file: IMG001.jpg IMG002.jpg
            travel
                file: trip.txt map.png
                sub_travel
                    file: packing_list.md

5. Conventions

These conventions follow the run-time stack model from our textbook [1], as best I remember it. Please let me know if you spot a mistake.

Registers:

  • R4: global data pointer (not needed in this program)
  • R5: frame pointer (points to the first local variable)
  • R6: stack pointer (points to the top element of the stack)
  • R7: return address (written by JSR and TRAP)

The stack frame of one function call (the stack grows toward lower addresses):

Address Contents
M[R5 - k] further local variables (if any)
M[R5 + 0] first local variable
M[R5 + 1] caller’s frame pointer
M[R5 + 2] return address
M[R5 + 3] return value (reserved even for void functions)
M[R5 + 4] first argument
M[R5 + 5] second argument, …

Other conventions:

  1. Arguments and local variables are accessed through R5 plus an offset, never through R6, because R6 moves whenever something is pushed.
  2. The caller pushes arguments from right to left, so the first argument ends up nearest the frame. On return, the callee leaves R6 pointing at the return value, and the caller pops the return value and the arguments.

Notes on this program:

  1. Each of print_folder(), print_file(), and print_space() has exactly one local variable (current, next, and i), stored at M[R5 + 0].
  2. main() does not build a frame and leaves R5 unset. This is fine here, because main never reads R5, and every callee saves and restores R5 itself.

II. LC-3 translation of the C functions

1. main()

2. print_folder()

3. print_file()

Saving R0 in a fixed memory location like PRINT_FILE_SAVE_R0 only works because print_file() is not recursive. A recursive function would overwrite the saved value on each nested call, so it would have to save registers on the stack instead.

4. print_space()

III. PRINT_A_CHAR and PRINT_A_STRING “system calls”

IV. Data

References

[1] Yale N. Patt and Sanjay J. Patel. Introduction to Computing Systems: From Bits & Gates to C/C++ & Beyond, 3rd edition. McGraw-Hill, 2019.
entry.summary: A review of LC-3 assembly, the run-time stack, recursion, linked lists, and binary trees, built around one complete program.

entry.title: The Gaussian Integral
entry.content:
This post introduces the Gaussian integral, starting from basic integration and building up to a probabilistic and linear-algebraic view of it.

I. The fundamental integral

The most basic Gaussian integral is

\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp \left(-\frac{1}{2}x^2 \right) dx = \sqrt{2\pi} ,\]

or equivalently, in the form of the standard Gaussian density,

\[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} x^2 \right) dx = 1 .\]

Here is how to compute it. Write \(I\) for the integral.

Step 1: square it

\[\begin{align*} I^2 &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} x^2 \right) dx \cdot \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} y^2 \right) dy \\[1ex] &= \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2}(x^2 + y^2) \right) dx \, dy . \end{align*}\]

The integrand is positive, so Tonelli’s theorem allows us to combine the two integrals into a double integral.

Step 2: switch to polar coordinates

Let

\[\left\{ \begin{aligned} x &= r \cos \theta \\ y &= r \sin \theta \end{aligned} \right. \qquad r \in [0, \infty), \ \theta \in [0, 2\pi) .\]

The Jacobian matrix of this map is

\[J(r, \theta) = \frac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (r, \theta)} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial r} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial \theta} \\[1.5ex] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial r} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial \theta} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos \theta & - r \sin \theta \\ \sin \theta & r \cos \theta \end{bmatrix} ,\]

so the area element transforms as

\[\begin{align*} dx \, dy &= \left\lvert \det J(r, \theta) \right\rvert \, dr \, d\theta \\[1ex] &= r \left( \cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta \right) dr \, d\theta \\[1ex] &= r \, dr \, d\theta . \end{align*}\]

Step 3: integrate

\[\begin{align*} I^2 &= \int_0^{2 \pi} \int_0^{\infty} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} r^2 \right) r \, dr \, d\theta \\[1ex] &= \int_0^{2 \pi} \left[ -\exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} r^2 \right) \right]_0^{\infty} d\theta \\[1ex] &= \int_0^{2 \pi} 1 \, d\theta = 2 \pi . \end{align*}\]

Since \(I > 0\),

\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} x^2 \right) dx = \sqrt{2 \pi} .\]

Shifting and scaling. Substituting \(x \mapsto (x - b)/\sqrt{a}\) gives, for any \(a > 0\) and \(b \in \mathbb{R}\),

\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp \left( -\frac{(x - b)^2}{2a} \right) dx = \sqrt{2 \pi a} ,\]

or, in the form of a Gaussian density,

\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi a}} \exp \left( -\frac{(x - b)^2}{2 a} \right) dx = 1 .\]

II. From one dimension to many

Now we generalize the univariate Gaussian integral to \(n\) dimensions.

Notation.

  1. \(\boldsymbol{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_n)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^n\) is a column vector.
  2. \(d\boldsymbol{x}\) denotes the volume element \(dx_1 \cdots dx_n\).
  3. For \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(\boldsymbol{x}) \, d \boldsymbol{x} = \idotsint_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x_1, \dots, x_n) \, dx_1 \cdots dx_n\).

Statement. Let \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) be symmetric positive definite, and let \(\boldsymbol{b} \in \mathbb{R}^n\). Then

\[\begin{equation} \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2} (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b})^\top A^{-1} (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b}) \right) d\boldsymbol{x} = \sqrt{ (2 \pi)^n \det A } . \label{eq:multivariate} \end{equation}\]

For \(n = 1\) and \(A = a\), this is exactly the shifted and scaled formula above.

Step 1: diagonalize

Since \(A\) is symmetric positive definite, so is \(A^{-1}\). By the spectral theorem [1],

\[A^{-1} = Q^\top \Lambda Q ,\]

where \(\Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)\) has positive diagonal entries and \(Q\) is orthogonal (\(Q^\top Q = Q Q^\top = I\)).

Change variables to

\[\boldsymbol{y} = Q (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b}) , \qquad \text{i.e.} \quad y_i = \sum_{j = 1}^{n} Q_{ij} (x_j - b_j) .\]

Then \(\partial y_i / \partial x_k = Q_{ik}\), so the Jacobian matrix is \(\partial \boldsymbol{y} / \partial \boldsymbol{x} = Q\). An orthogonal matrix satisfies \(\det(Q)^2 = \det(Q^\top Q) = 1\), so \(\det Q = \pm 1\). (It can be \(-1\), for a reflection. That is why the absolute value matters.) Hence

\[d \boldsymbol{y} = \left\lvert \det Q \right\rvert d \boldsymbol{x} = d \boldsymbol{x} .\]

Substituting,

\[\begin{align*} &\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2} (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b})^\top A^{-1} (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b}) \right) d\boldsymbol{x} \\[1ex] ={} &\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b})^\top Q^\top \Lambda Q (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b}) \right) d \boldsymbol{x} \\[1ex] ={} &\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} \big(Q (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b}) \big)^\top \Lambda \big(Q (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b}) \big) \right) d \boldsymbol{x} \\[1ex] ={} &\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol{y}^\top \Lambda \boldsymbol{y} \right) d \boldsymbol{y} . \end{align*}\]

Step 2: separate the variables

Because \(\Lambda\) is diagonal,

\[\boldsymbol{y}^\top \Lambda \boldsymbol{y} = \begin{bmatrix} y_1 & \cdots & y_n \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1 & & \\ & \ddots & \\ & & \lambda_n \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ \vdots \\ y_n \end{bmatrix} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i y_i^2 ,\]

so the exponential factors into a product, and so does the integral:

\[\begin{align*} \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol{y}^\top \Lambda \boldsymbol{y} \right) d \boldsymbol{y} &= \idotsint_{\mathbb{R}^n} \prod_{i=1}^{n} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} \lambda_i y_i^2 \right) dy_1 \cdots dy_n \\[1ex] &= \prod_{i=1}^{n} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} \lambda_i y_i^2 \right) dy_i . \end{align*}\]

Step 3: use the one-dimensional result

Each factor is a one-dimensional Gaussian integral with \(a = 1/\lambda_i\):

\[\prod_{i=1}^{n} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp \left( -\frac{y_i^2}{2 \lambda_i^{-1}} \right) dy_i = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \sqrt{\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda_i}} = \frac{(2 \pi)^{n/2}}{\sqrt{\det \Lambda}} .\]

Finally, from \(A^{-1} = Q^\top \Lambda Q\),

\[\frac{1}{\det A} = \det (A^{-1}) = \det(Q^\top) \det(\Lambda) \det(Q) = \det(Q)^2 \det \Lambda = \det \Lambda .\]

Putting everything together,

\[\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2} (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b})^\top A^{-1} (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b}) \right) d\boldsymbol{x} = \frac{(2 \pi)^{n/2}}{\sqrt{\det \Lambda}} = \sqrt{ (2 \pi)^n \det A } ,\]

which proves \(\eqref{eq:multivariate}\). \(\blacksquare\)

III. Probability and linear algebra

1. The univariate Gaussian distribution

If \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\), its density integrates to one:

\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(x) \, dx = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} \exp \left( -\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) dx = 1 .\]

This is just the shifted and scaled formula from Part I: the mean \(\mu\) plays the role of the shift \(b\), and the variance \(\sigma^2\) plays the role of the scale \(a\).

2. The multivariate Gaussian distribution

We write a random vector in bold capitals, \(\boldsymbol{X} = (X_1, \dots, X_n)^\top\). Each component \(X_i\) is a random variable. A specific value of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is written in bold lowercase, \(\boldsymbol{x}\).

If \(\boldsymbol{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \Sigma)\) with a positive definite covariance matrix \(\Sigma\), then by \(\eqref{eq:multivariate}\) with \(A = \Sigma\) and \(\boldsymbol{b} = \boldsymbol{\mu}\),

\[\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol{x}) \, d \boldsymbol{x} = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^n \det \Sigma}} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} (\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \Sigma^{-1}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\right) d \boldsymbol{x} = 1 .\]

The interesting part is the change of variables that simplified the quadratic form in the exponent. It has a clear probabilistic meaning.

(1) Diagonalizing \(\Sigma^{-1}\): the PCA view

Write

\[\Sigma^{-1} = Q^\top \Lambda Q ,\]

where the rows of the orthogonal matrix \(Q\) are eigenvectors of \(\Sigma^{-1}\), and \(\Lambda\) holds the corresponding eigenvalues. The eigenvectors of \(\Sigma^{-1}\) are the same as those of \(\Sigma\), but each eigenvalue is inverted: \(\Sigma = Q^\top \Lambda^{-1} Q\).

This is exactly the core idea of principal component analysis (PCA) [2]. We find the principal axes of the distribution and rotate the coordinate system to align with them. The variance along the \(i\)-th axis is \(1/\lambda_i\), so the direction of largest variance belongs to the smallest eigenvalue of \(\Sigma^{-1}\).

(2) The change of variables

Apply

\[\boldsymbol{y} = Q (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}) , \qquad \text{equivalently} \qquad \boldsymbol{Y} = Q (\boldsymbol{X} - \boldsymbol{\mu}) .\]

This centers and rotates the coordinate system, and the quadratic form becomes

\[(\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}) = \boldsymbol{y}^\top \Lambda \boldsymbol{y} .\]

The covariance of the new random vector is

\[\mathrm{Cov}(\boldsymbol{Y}) = \mathbb{E}\left[\boldsymbol{Y} \boldsymbol{Y}^\top\right] = Q \, \Sigma \, Q^\top = Q \left( Q^\top \Lambda^{-1} Q \right) Q^\top = \Lambda^{-1} ,\]

which is diagonal. So the components \(Y_1, \dots, Y_n\) are uncorrelated, with \(\mathrm{Var}(Y_i) = 1/\lambda_i\). Going from \(\boldsymbol{X}\) to \(\boldsymbol{Y}\) decorrelates the coordinates.

(3) Uncorrelated vs. independent

In general, uncorrelated random variables need not be independent. But for a jointly Gaussian random vector, uncorrelated components are independent. (Marginally Gaussian is not enough: the vector must be jointly Gaussian.) Here \(\boldsymbol{Y}\) is an affine function of a Gaussian vector, so it is jointly Gaussian.

You can see this directly from the density, which factors into a product of one-dimensional Gaussians:

\[f_{\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{y}) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\lambda_i^{-1}}} \exp\left( -\frac{y_i^2}{2\lambda_i^{-1}} \right) = \prod_{i=1}^n \mathcal{N}\!\left(y_i;\, 0,\, \lambda_i^{-1}\right) .\]

This factorization is exactly what made the integral in Part II easy to compute.

Thanks to ChatGPT, which helped me organize my words.

References

[1] David Vogan. “Proof of the spectral theorem.” Lecture notes, MIT, 2013.

[2] Jonathon Shlens. “A Tutorial on Principal Component Analysis.” 2005.
entry.summary: From the one-dimensional Gaussian integral to the multivariate case, with a probabilistic and linear-algebraic view.

entry.title: The Central Limit Theorem
entry.content:
Thanks to 子预. His article helped me a lot in understanding this topic [1].

This post gives a short, mostly self-contained proof of the Central Limit Theorem (CLT). It is not fully rigorous: I state two standard results from analysis without proving them.

The CLT is one of the most important results in probability theory. It says that the normalized sum of many independent random variables tends to a normal distribution, whatever the distribution of each variable is. This is why the bell curve shows up so often in nature: many small, independent sources of randomness add up to a predictable pattern.

The statement

Theorem (Lindeberg–Lévy CLT). Let \(X_1, X_2, \dots\) be i.i.d. (independent and identically distributed) random variables with \(\mathbb{E}[X_j] = \mu\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(X_j) = \sigma^2\), where \(0 < \sigma^2 < \infty\). Define

\[Z_n = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^n X_j - n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt{n}} .\]

Then for every \(\tau \in \mathbb{R}\),

\[\lim_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}(Z_n \leq \tau) = \Phi(\tau) = \int_{-\infty}^{\tau} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-x^2/2} \, dx ,\]

or, equivalently, \(Z_n \xrightarrow{D} \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\).

Notes.

  • The name Lindeberg–Lévy refers to this version of the theorem, which needs i.i.d. variables with finite variance.
  • A more general version, the Lindeberg–Feller CLT, drops the “identically distributed” assumption and replaces it with the weaker Lindeberg condition.

1. The road map

We use characteristic functions. The characteristic function of a random variable \(X\) is

\[\varphi_X(t) = \mathbb{E}\left[e^{itX}\right], \qquad t \in \mathbb{R}.\]

It always exists, because \(\lvert e^{itX} \rvert = 1\). The proof rests on two classical facts, which I state without proof:

  1. Uniqueness. The characteristic function determines the distribution: if \(\varphi_X(t) = \varphi_Y(t)\) for all \(t\), then \(X\) and \(Y\) have the same distribution. (This is the Fourier inversion theorem in disguise.)
  2. Lévy’s continuity theorem. If \(\varphi_{Z_n}(t) \to \varphi_Z(t)\) for every \(t\), then \(Z_n \xrightarrow{D} Z\). (See Durrett [2], Section 3.3, for proofs of both facts.)

Uniqueness alone is not enough. We never have \(\varphi_{Z_n} = \varphi_N\) exactly for a finite \(n\), so we need the continuity theorem to turn pointwise convergence of characteristic functions into convergence in distribution.

So the plan is:

  1. compute the characteristic function of \(N \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\);
  2. show that \(\varphi_{Z_n}(t) \to \varphi_N(t)\) for every \(t\);
  3. apply Lévy’s continuity theorem.

We use two simple properties of characteristic functions, which are proved in the appendix:

  1. Affine maps: \(\varphi_{aX + b}(t) = e^{ibt} \, \varphi_X(at)\).
  2. Independence: if \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, then \(\varphi_{X + Y}(t) = \varphi_X(t) \, \varphi_Y(t)\).

2. The characteristic function of \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\)

Let \(N \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\). We want to show

\[\varphi_N(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{itx} \, \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-x^2/2} \, dx = e^{-t^2/2}.\]

The quick (heuristic) way. Complete the square in the exponent:

\[\begin{align*} \varphi_N(t) &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{-\frac{1}{2}x^2 + itx} \, dx \\[1ex] &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{-\frac{1}{2}(x - it)^2 + \frac{1}{2}(it)^2} \, dx \\[1ex] &= e^{-\frac{1}{2}t^2} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{-\frac{1}{2}(x - it)^2} \, dx . \end{align*}\]

The remaining integral is the Gaussian integral shifted by the imaginary constant \(it\). It still equals \(\sqrt{2\pi}\), but justifying this requires contour integration (Cauchy’s theorem). A plain real change of variables does not work.

A rigorous way without complex analysis. Since \(\mathbb{E}\lvert N \rvert < \infty\), we may differentiate under the integral sign:

\[\begin{align*} \varphi_N'(t) &= \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} ix \, e^{itx} \, \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-x^2/2} \, dx \\[1ex] &= \frac{i}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{itx} \, d\!\left(-e^{-x^2/2}\right) \\[1ex] &= \frac{i}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \left( \Big[-e^{itx} e^{-x^2/2}\Big]_{-\infty}^{+\infty} + \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} it \, e^{itx} e^{-x^2/2} \, dx \right) \\[1ex] &= -t \, \varphi_N(t). \end{align*}\]

This is a first-order linear ODE with \(\varphi_N(0) = 1\). Its unique solution is \(\varphi_N(t) = e^{-t^2/2}\).

3. The characteristic function of \(Z_n\)

Step 1: standardize

Define the standardized variables

\[Y_j = \frac{X_j - \mu}{\sigma}, \qquad \text{so that} \quad \mathbb{E}[Y_j] = 0, \quad \mathbb{E}[Y_j^2] = \mathrm{Var}(Y_j) = 1 .\]

Then

\[Z_n = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{j=1}^n Y_j .\]

The \(Y_j\) are still i.i.d., so they share one characteristic function, which we write as \(\varphi_Y\).

Step 2: expand \(\varphi_Y\) near zero

The original version of this post expanded \(e^{itY}\) as an infinite Taylor series and swapped \(\mathbb{E}\) with the sum. That is not allowed here, because it needs all moments of \(Y\) to exist, and we only assumed a finite second moment.

The correct tool is a second-order expansion. Since \(\mathbb{E}[Y^2] < \infty\), \(\varphi_Y\) is twice continuously differentiable, with

\[\varphi_Y(0) = 1, \qquad \varphi_Y'(0) = i\,\mathbb{E}[Y] = 0, \qquad \varphi_Y''(0) = -\mathbb{E}[Y^2] = -1 .\]

Taylor’s theorem then gives

\[\varphi_Y(t) = 1 - \frac{t^2}{2} + o(t^2) \qquad \text{as } t \to 0 .\]

Step 3: multiply

By the two properties of characteristic functions (independence, then the affine map with \(a = 1/\sqrt{n}\), \(b = 0\)):

\[\begin{align*} \varphi_{Z_n}(t) &= \varphi_{\sum_j Y_j}\!\left( \frac{t}{\sqrt{n}} \right) = \left( \varphi_Y\!\left( \frac{t}{\sqrt{n}} \right) \right)^n \\[1ex] &= \left( 1 - \frac{t^2}{2n} + o\!\left( \frac{1}{n} \right) \right)^n \qquad (n \to \infty,\ t \text{ fixed}). \end{align*}\]

Step 4: take the limit

For fixed \(t\), write \(c_n = n\left(\varphi_Y(t/\sqrt{n}) - 1\right)\). The expansion above shows \(c_n \to -t^2/2\). A standard fact (which also holds for complex \(c_n\)) is

\[c_n \to c \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \left( 1 + \frac{c_n}{n} \right)^n \to e^{c} .\]

Therefore

\[\lim_{n \to \infty} \varphi_{Z_n}(t) = e^{-t^2/2} = \varphi_N(t) \qquad \text{for every } t \in \mathbb{R} .\]

4. Conclusion

We have shown that \(\varphi_{Z_n}(t) \to \varphi_N(t)\) for every \(t\), and \(\varphi_N\) is the characteristic function of \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\). By Lévy’s continuity theorem,

\[Z_n \xrightarrow{D} \mathcal{N}(0, 1) . \qquad \blacksquare\]

This completes the proof of the CLT for i.i.d. variables with finite, nonzero variance.

Appendix: two properties of characteristic functions

Affine maps. For constants \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\),

\[\varphi_{aX+b}(t) = \mathbb{E}\left[e^{it(aX+b)}\right] = e^{itb} \, \mathbb{E}\left[e^{i(ta)X}\right] = e^{itb} \, \varphi_X(at) .\]

Independence. If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent with densities \(f_X, f_Y\), their joint density factors as \(f_{X,Y}(x, y) = f_X(x) f_Y(y)\). So for any (bounded, measurable) functions \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\),

\[\begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[\alpha(X)\beta(Y)] &= \iint f_{X,Y}(x, y) \, \alpha(x) \beta(y) \, dx \, dy \\[1ex] &= \iint f_X(x) f_Y(y) \, \alpha(x) \beta(y) \, dx \, dy \\[1ex] &= \int f_X(x) \, \alpha(x) \, dx \cdot \int f_Y(y) \, \beta(y) \, dy \\[1ex] &= \mathbb{E}[\alpha(X)] \cdot \mathbb{E}[\beta(Y)] . \end{align*}\]

The same identity holds without densities, but it is easiest to see in this case. Taking \(\alpha(x) = e^{itx}\) and \(\beta(y) = e^{ity}\),

\[\varphi_{X + Y}(t) = \mathbb{E}\left[e^{itX} e^{itY}\right] = \mathbb{E}\left[e^{itX}\right] \mathbb{E}\left[e^{itY}\right] = \varphi_X(t) \, \varphi_Y(t) .\]

By induction, the characteristic function of a sum of \(n\) independent variables is the product of their characteristic functions.

References

[1] 子预. Article on the central limit theorem (in Chinese). Zhihu.

[2] Rick Durrett. Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th edition. Cambridge University Press, 2019.
entry.summary: A short proof of the Lindeberg–Lévy central limit theorem using characteristic functions.
